# Generating Random Numbers

## Sangeet Satpathy, Winter 2026

### Motivation

Throughout CS109, we have been sampling from distributions of random variables. We usually let another library handle it. Yet, at the core of this sampling is the ability to generate a random number. This is because, when sampling from any PDF or PMF, all distributions can be thought of as a sum of many different “bernoulli trials”, in some sense. There are various methods for sampling from a distribution, once we have the ability to output a probability from 0 to 1\. In class, we have already seen **rejection sampling**, where we just generate random numbers, rejecting any samples that are not in our “desired” probability range. 

But how do computers come up with this probability from 0 and 1? This quarter, I’ve been taking CS107E: Computer Systems from the Ground Up, so I’ve been very involved with low level firmware programming. So something **didn’t add up for me.** Computers are deterministic. So how do they come up with random numbers?

For my project, I will explain my learnings, and then show how I implemented a mimicry of true randomness\!

### Part 1: Overview of Pseudo-Random Generation

It turns out that when we call a lot of basic random functions, they aren’t actually random. Instead, they simply give off the appearance of being random. In reality, they are linear patterns. There are two algorithms to note: LCG (linear congruential generator) and LFSR (linear feedback shift register).

LCG:  
![][image1]  
Essentially, we start at a given number, X\_0. Every time we call rand(), we simply perform the operation above, and store the new X\_i. And it’s cyclical in nature, since once our X is above m, the mod m kicks in and we wrap around. The values a, c, and m are set by the language libraries.

This is actually why we can ‘seed’ our random values. This just simply says, “whenever we call this function again, start at this value\!” Not so random, is it? This is also why people advise not to use any of the standard random() functions for anything that needs any amount of security. An attacker can easily analyze a couple of calls to the random function, and determine what the pattern is.

[LFSR](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ks1pw1X22y4):  
The idea here is that you have an array of k bits. Each ‘cycle’, you shift all of the bits one position to the right; And then, to add SOME ‘randomness’, the NEW INCOMING BITS (from the left hand side) are a function of some of the other bits (usually an XOR). I won’t go too much into detail into this, as it is not really the main focus of my project.  
However, the point is, this is not random\! 

### Part 2: Randomness from the Outside World

The fact of the matter is that computers cannot generate randomness from within. They must look to the world to “detect” randomness. Examples of where randomness is detected includes: radioactive decay of isotopes, airwave static, and the behavior of subatomic particles. Most modern computer systems keep an “entropy pool”; in addition to measuring random events in the subatomic world, they keep a record of events such as interrupt timings, user input, and network packet timings.

For my project, I decided to focus on generating random numbers from interrupt timings — and handily, since I’m in CS107E, I already have a full working interrupt handler library for keyboard events\! I used the **differences in keyboard interrupt times** as my “entropy source”.

Now, keyboard timings are not truly random. Humans have an average typing speed. However, the tiny variations in this **are** random. However, this begs the question, why can’t we just use any sequence of bitstrings? What exactly IS randomness? Let’s dive into some information theory.

### Part 3: Information Theory

I’ve been talking a lot about “harvesting randomness”. But it would provide some insight to actually define what randomness is. We define a bitstring to be random if we **cannot “compress”** it. In other words, we cannot describe the string with a shorter variation of it. This is called ‘Kolmogorov Complexity’ (take CS154\!), but for now, you can think of “11110000” being able to be described somehow as “4 1’s and 4 0’s” which can be encoded in less bits.  
It has been proved that we can't actually ever tell if a string **is** **or isn’t** compressible. However, instead of being absolute about it, we can measure, “is it *kinda* random?” This is exactly what entropy does. Yes, the entropy we have covered in class. In CS109, we were introduced to entropy as a measure of the “expected surprise” of a distribution. In information theory, they say entropy is the measure of how much “information” is contained in the distribution, which may be a little misleading. What this means is that, “**how many yes/no questions would you have to ask to understand the full distribution?**”. But personally, I think these definitions are harder to understand, so I think relating it back to Kolmogorov Complexity is much more useful.

Back to keyboard timings. Even if we have several keyboard presses, we have a very low **entropy** — that’s because most of the keyboard deltas will follow some underlying pattern. People tend to write at relatively constant speed, and some letters will be more common than others — there are many dependencies at play. This means that, if I were to know these dependencies, I could **compress the keyboard timings** into less bits – and relating back to Kolmogorov Complexity, a highly compressible message has a very low randomness.

This tells us two things: Firstly, When I harvest the entropy of my keystrokes, I must get a LOT of key data. Secondly, I need some way to “distill” the randomness, so that my final, random number doesn’t have any of the predictable parts. How do I do this distillation?

### Part 4: [SHA](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=f9EbD6iY9zI)

SHA-256 is a secure hash function that converts any string into a **unique**, 256 bit string. By the pigeonhole principle, we are guaranteed that there will be collisions (two strings that convert to the same 256 bit string). However, the beauty of SHA is that it would take SO FRICKING LONG to find two strings that convert to the same hash (billions of years with current technology\!). This makes it ideal for digital signatures — once you change a document, the hash would have changed, and any malicious person would be unable to manipulate the input data to try and get the original hash (to make it look unchanged).  
**This is the entropy distillation we want**. While SHA gets rid of lots of data, it is mathematically designed so that EVERY BIT has a dependence on EVERY BIT OF THE OUTPUT. This means that changing a SINGLE BIT of the input results in a huge change in the output (the “Avalanche Effect”)\!   
Here’s how that relates to entropy: in a distribution, entropy is maximized when all the outcomes are as close to equally likely as possible. This means that an entropy-maximizing hash function would take all the infinitely possible inputs and map them UNIFORMLY onto the 2256 possibilities. As a result, bitstrings 00001 and 00010, which are not so different from each other, should mathematically be very different, in an ideal, entropy-maximizing function. This is what SHA is good at\!

So how does SHA do this? The math is very complicated, but these are the key component functions: [XOR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exclusive_or), [Rotation Shifting](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/rotate-bits-of-an-integer/), [Majority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majority_function) (takes 3 bits; whichever bit is the majority of these 3 is the output), and Choice (takes 3 bits; the first bit determines which of the next two bits to select; if it’s a 0, it selects the 2nd bit, and if its a 1, it selects the 3rd bit).

The goal of SHA is to create all these bit interdependencies; but also, we want to make sure attackers can never reverse engineer them. From my understanding, the XOR and rotation shifts are essential for making the interdependencies of the bits; while the Majority and Choice Functions provide the ‘non-linearity’ – you can’t easily reverse them. Doing only XORs would mean it’s easy to reverse engineer; doing only majority/choice functions would mean each bit is independent, and we would lose a lot of entropy.

For my project, I implemented a rudimentary version of the SHA algorithm using these components. A lot of time was spent pitching a prospective algorithm to Google Gemini, and it poked holes in my approach, and I would revise my algorithm. For my project demo, please see my video\!
